{{Short description|Physics concept regarding radiation transparency and attenuation}}
{{Other uses|Optical depth (astrophysics)}}

[[File:Aerosol Optical Depth (haze) at Geronimo Creek Observatory, Texas (1990-2016).jpg|thumb|Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) at 830 nm measured with an LED sun photometer (1990–2016) at Geronimo Creek Observatory, Texas. Measurements were recorded at or near solar noon. Peaks indicate smoke, dust, and smog events.]]

In [[physics]], '''optical depth''' or '''optical thickness''' is the [[natural logarithm]] of the ratio of incident to transmitted [[radiant power]] through a material.
Thus, the larger the optical depth, the smaller the fraction of transmitted radiant power through the medium. 
'''Spectral optical depth''' or '''spectral optical thickness''' is the natural logarithm of the ratio of incident to transmitted [[Radiant power|spectral radiant power]] through a material.<ref name=GoldBook>{{GoldBookRef|title=Absorbance|file=A00028|accessdate=2024-01-01}}</ref> 

Optical depth is a [[Dimensionless quantity|dimensionless quantity]]. Although it is a [[Monotonic function|monotonically]] increasing function of path length, it is not a physical distance itself, approaching zero as the path length vanishes. The use of the term "optical density" for optical depth is discouraged.<ref name=GoldBook />

In [[chemistry]], a closely related quantity called [[absorbance]] (or decadic absorbance) is used instead of optical depth. Absorbance uses the [[common logarithm]] (base 10) of the ratio of incident to transmitted radiant power. It relates to optical depth by a factor of {{math|''log''<sub>''e''</sub>(10)}}.

== Mathematical definitions ==
=== Optical depth ===
The optical depth of a material, denoted by <math>\tau</math>, is defined as:<ref>{{cite book|author=Christopher Robert Kitchin|year=1987|title=Stars, Nebulae and the Interstellar Medium: Observational Physics and Astrophysics|publisher=[[CRC Press]]}}</ref>
:<math>\tau = \ln\!\left(\frac{\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{i}}{\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{t}}\right) = -\ln T</math>
where
* <math>\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{i}</math> is the [[radiant flux]] received (incident) by that material;
* <math>\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{t}</math> is the [[radiant flux]] transmitted by that material;
* <math>T</math> is the [[transmittance]] of that material.

The decadic absorbance <math>A</math> is related to optical depth by:
:<math>\tau = A \ln 10 \approx 2.3026 A</math>

=== Spectral optical depth ===
The spectral optical depth in frequency (<math>\tau_\nu</math>) or in wavelength (<math>\tau_\lambda</math>) is given by:<ref name=GoldBook />
:<math>\tau_\nu = \ln\!\left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\nu}^\mathrm{i}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\nu}^\mathrm{t}}\right) = -\ln T_\nu</math>
:<math>\tau_\lambda = \ln\!\left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\lambda}^\mathrm{i}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\lambda}^\mathrm{t}}\right) = -\ln T_\lambda</math>
where
* <math>\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\nu}^\mathrm{i}</math> and <math>\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\nu}^\mathrm{t}</math> are the incident and transmitted spectral radiant fluxes in frequency;
* <math>T_\nu</math> is the spectral transmittance in frequency;
* <math>\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\lambda}^\mathrm{i}</math> and <math>\Phi_{\mathrm{e},\lambda}^\mathrm{t}</math> are the incident and transmitted spectral radiant fluxes in wavelength;
* <math>T_\lambda</math> is the spectral transmittance in wavelength.

Spectral absorbance relates to spectral optical depth via:
:<math>\tau_\nu = A_\nu \ln 10</math>
:<math>\tau_\lambda = A_\lambda \ln 10</math>

== Relationship with attenuation ==

=== Attenuation ===
{{Main article|Attenuation}}
Optical depth quantifies the attenuation of transmitted radiant power in a medium. Attenuation can occur via absorption, scattering, reflection, and other physical processes. 

According to the [[Beer–Lambert law]], the transmitted flux decays exponentially with optical depth:
:<math>T = e^{-\tau}</math>

The fractional attenuation (<math>\text{ATT}</math>) is given by:
:<math>\text{ATT} = \frac{\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{att}}{\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{i}} = 1 - e^{-\tau} + E</math>
where <math>E = \Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{e}/\Phi_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{i}</math> is the relative emittance of the medium. For optically thin media (<math>\tau \ll 1</math>) with negligible emission (<math>E \ll \tau</math>), attenuation reduces approximately to the optical depth itself:
:<math>\text{ATT} \approx \tau</math>

=== Attenuation coefficient ===
The optical depth along a path of length <math>l</math> is related to the local [[attenuation coefficient]] <math>\alpha(z)</math> by:
:<math>\tau = \int_0^l \alpha(z)\, \mathrm{d}z</math>

If <math>\alpha</math> is uniform along the path, the relation simplifies to:
:<math>\tau = \alpha l</math>

In terms of the attenuation [[Cross section (physics)|cross-section]] <math>\sigma</math> per particle and number density <math>n(z)</math>:
:<math>\tau = \int_0^l \sigma n(z)\, \mathrm{d}z = \sigma N</math>
where <math>N = \int_0^l n(z)\,\mathrm{d}z</math> is the [[column density]] along the line of sight.

== Applications ==

=== Atomic physics ===
In [[atomic physics]], the spectral optical depth of a cloud of resonant two-level atoms can be determined from quantum-mechanical dipole transitions:
:<math>\tau_\nu = \frac{d^2 n \nu}{2 c \hbar \varepsilon_0 A \gamma} \mathcal{L}(\nu)</math>
where
* <math>d</math> is the [[transition dipole moment]];
* <math>n</math> is the total number of atoms;
* <math>\nu</math> is the frequency of the incident radiation;
* <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]];
* <math>\hbar</math> is the [[reduced Planck constant]];
* <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is the [[vacuum permittivity]];
* <math>A</math> is the cross-sectional area of the beam;
* <math>\gamma</math> is the [[natural linewidth]] of the atomic transition;
* <math>\mathcal{L}(\nu)</math> is the normalized spectral line profile shape.

=== Atmospheric sciences ===
{{See also|Beer–Lambert law}}
In [[atmospheric sciences]], optical depth often refers to a vertical path extending from Earth's surface to outer space. For a slanted line of sight at zenith angle <math>\theta</math>, the slant optical depth <math>\tau</math> relates to vertical optical depth <math>\tau'</math> by the [[airmass]] factor <math>m</math>:
:<math>\tau = m \tau' \approx \tau' \sec\theta</math>
yielding a total transmittance of:
:<math>T = e^{-\tau} = e^{-m\tau'}</math>

The total atmospheric optical depth encompasses contributions from [[Rayleigh scattering]], [[aerosol]] optical depth (AOD), and trace gas [[absorption (electromagnetic radiation)|absorption]], routinely measured using [[Sun photometer|Sun photometers]].

With altitude <math>z</math>, optical depth in an exponential atmosphere scales as:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=A First Course in Atmospheric Radiation|last=Petty|first=Grant W.|year=2006|publisher=Sundog Publishing|isbn=9780972903318}}</ref>
:<math>\tau(z) = k_\text{a} w_1 \rho_0 H e^{-z/H}</math>
giving a sea-level vertical optical depth of:
:<math>\tau(0) = k_\text{a} w_1 \rho_0 H</math>

where:
* <math>k_\text{a}</math> is the absorption coefficient;
* <math>w_1</math> is the species mixing ratio;
* <math>\rho_0</math> is the air density at sea level;
* <math>H</math> is the atmospheric [[scale height]];
* <math>z</math> is the altitude above sea level.

For a uniform plane-parallel cloud layer, optical depth can be parameterized as:<ref name=":0" />
:<math>\tau = Q_\text{e} \left[\frac{9\pi L^2 H N}{16\rho_\text{l}^2}\right]^{1/3}</math>
where:
* <math>Q_\text{e}</math> is the extinction efficiency;
* <math>L</math> is the [[liquid water path]];
* <math>H</math> is the geometrical thickness of the cloud;
* <math>N</math> is the droplet number concentration;
* <math>\rho_\text{l}</math> is the density of liquid water.

Thus, for a constant cloud thickness and total liquid water content, optical depth scales with droplet concentration as <math>\tau \propto N^{1/3}</math>.<ref name=":0" />

=== Astronomy ===
{{Main article|Optical depth (astrophysics)}}
In astronomy, optical depth governs radiation escape from stellar atmospheres, planetary rings, and nebulae. In stellar physics, the [[photosphere]] is defined as the atmospheric depth where <math>\tau \approx 2/3</math>, representing the mean surface from which thermal photons escape into space.

For [[planetary rings]], optical depth measures the fraction of light blocked by ring material during stellar occultations.

[[File:PIA22737-Mars-2018DustStorm-MCS-MRO-Animation-20181030.webm|thumb|[[Atmosphere of Mars|Mars global dust storm]] optical depth (<math>\tau</math>) evolution from May to September 2018, measured by the [[Mars Climate Sounder]] on the [[Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter]].]]
